claim: Rett syndrome is caused by mutations in MECP2.
source: Rett syndrome (RTT) is caused by mutations in the X-linked gene encoding methyl CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) (Amir et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Amir et al., 1999

claim: Deleting Mecp2 only from GABAergic inhibitory neurons in mice replicates most of the Rett syndrome phenotype.
source: Surprisingly, despite the diversity of these features, we have found that deleting Mecp2 only from GABAergic inhibitory neurons in mice replicates most of this phenotype.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the authors' research

claim: Genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice enhanced inhibitory signaling.
source: Here we show that genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice enhanced inhibitory signaling, extended lifespan, and rescued ataxia, apraxia, and social abnormalities but did not rescue tremor or anxiety.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice extended lifespan.
source: Here we show that genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice enhanced inhibitory signaling, extended lifespan, and rescued ataxia, apraxia, and social abnormalities but did not rescue tremor or anxiety.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice rescued ataxia.
source: Here we show that genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice enhanced inhibitory signaling, extended lifespan, and rescued ataxia, apraxia, and social abnormalities but did not rescue tremor or anxiety.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice rescued apraxia.
source: Here we show that genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice enhanced inhibitory signaling, extended lifespan, and rescued ataxia, apraxia, and social abnormalities but did not rescue tremor or anxiety.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice rescued social abnormalities.
source: Here we show that genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice enhanced inhibitory signaling, extended lifespan, and rescued ataxia, apraxia, and social abnormalities but did not rescue tremor or anxiety.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

source: Here we show that genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice enhanced inhibitory signaling, extended lifespan, and rescued ataxia, apraxia, and social abnormalities but did not rescue tremor or anxiety.

source: Here we show that genetically restoring Mecp2 expression only in GABAergic neurons of male Mecp2 null mice enhanced inhibitory signaling, extended lifespan, and rescued ataxia, apraxia, and social abnormalities but did not rescue tremor or anxiety.

claim: Female Mecp2+/- mice showed a less dramatic but still substantial rescue when Mecp2 was restored in GABAergic neurons.
source: Female Mecp2+/- mice showed a less dramatic but still substantial rescue.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study

claim: Alterations in excitatory/inhibitory balance are postulated to underlie autism.
source: Alterations in this excitatory/inhibitory balance are postulated to underlie a number of neuropsychiatric disorders, such as autism (Vattikuti and Chow, 2010; Gogolla et al., 2009; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Alterations in excitatory/inhibitory balance are postulated to underlie schizophrenia.
source: Alterations in this excitatory/inhibitory balance are postulated to underlie a number of neuropsychiatric disorders, such as autism (Vattikuti and Chow, 2010; Gogolla et al., 2009; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003), schizophrenia (Belforte et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Belforte et al., 2010

claim: Alterations in excitatory/inhibitory balance are postulated to underlie Rett syndrome.
source: Alterations in this excitatory/inhibitory balance are postulated to underlie a number of neuropsychiatric disorders, such as autism (Vattikuti and Chow, 2010; Gogolla et al., 2009; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003), schizophrenia (Belforte et al., 2010), and Rett syndrome (Dani et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dani et al., 2005

claim: Dysfunctional GABAergic signaling has been implicated in Rett syndrome.
source: Dysfunctional GABAergic signaling has been implicated in multiple neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders (Siniatchkin and Koepp, 2009; Pizzarelli and Cherubini, 2011), including Rett syndrome (Chao et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chao et al., 2010

claim: Deletion of Mecp2 solely in GABAergic neurons is sufficient to reproduce the majority of the Rett-like features of the constitutive Mecp2-null mouse.
source: In fact, deletion of Mecp2 solely in GABAergic neurons is sufficient to reproduce the majority of the Rett-like features of the constitutive Mecp2-null mouse, including ataxia, stereotyped behaviors, seizures, breathing abnormalities, and premature death (Chao et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chao et al., 2010

claim: MeCP2 is a protein that is highly expressed throughout the brain.
source: Rett syndrome (RTT) is caused by mutations in the X-linked gene encoding methyl CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) (Amir et al., 1999), a protein that is highly expressed throughout the brain and involved in chromatin modulation (Baker et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker et al., 2013

claim: MeCP2 is involved in chromatin modulation.
source: Rett syndrome (RTT) is caused by mutations in the X-linked gene encoding methyl CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) (Amir et al., 1999), a protein that is highly expressed throughout the brain and involved in chromatin modulation (Baker et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker et al., 2013

claim: Disease-causing MECP2 mutations cause a rapidly fatal neonatal encephalopathy in human males.
source: RTT is notable for the variety of different behaviors it affects: disease-causing MECP2 mutations cause a rapidly fatal neonatal encephalopathy in human males
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about RTT

claim: Females with disease-causing MECP2 mutations develop normally until around one year of age, at which point they regress developmentally.
source: disease-causing MECP2 mutations cause a rapidly fatal neonatal encephalopathy in human males but allow females to develop normally until around one year of age, at which point they regress developmentally, losing acquired language, social, and motor milestones
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about RTT

claim: Mecp2 knockout mice replicate all features of the human Rett syndrome disease.
source: Mecp2 knockout mice replicate all these features of the human disease (Chen et al., 2001; Guy et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2001 and Guy et al., 2001

claim: Male Mecp2-null mice develop symptoms and die within the first five months of life.
source: Mecp2 knockout mice replicate all these features of the human disease (Chen et al., 2001; Guy et al., 2001), with male Mecp2-null mice developing symptoms and dying within the first five months of life
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2001 and Guy et al., 2001

claim: Mecp2-heterozygous females develop progressive neurological dysfunction with a later onset.
source: Mecp2-heterozygous females develop progressive neurological dysfunction with a later onset, because random X chromosome inactivation preserves expression of wildtype Mecp2 in more than half of their cells (Samaco et al., 2013; Young and Zoghbi, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to Samaco et al., 2013 and Young and Zoghbi, 2004

claim: RTT is not a neurodegenerative disorder.
source: While Mecp2-mutant male and female mice develop profound disabilities, RTT is not a neurodegenerative disorder.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about RTT

claim: Mecp2-null neurons are rendered partly dysfunctional but are still present, active, and properly located developmentally.
source: Mecp2-null neurons are rendered partly dysfunctional but are still present, active, and properly located developmentally (Chao et al., 2007; 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chao et al., 2007 and 2010

claim: Viaat-Cre is not expressed in glial cells.
source: To confirm that Viaat-Cre was not expressed in glial cells or microglia (Lioy et al., 2011; Derecki et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015), we crossed Viaat-Cre male mice with female ROSA-LSL-YFP transgenics and co-stained for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), a glial marker, and ionized calcium binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba1), a marker of microglia. As expected, we observed no colocalization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry showing no colocalization with glial markers

claim: Viaat-Cre is not expressed in microglia.
source: To confirm that Viaat-Cre was not expressed in glial cells or microglia (Lioy et al., 2011; Derecki et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015), we crossed Viaat-Cre male mice with female ROSA-LSL-YFP transgenics and co-stained for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), a glial marker, and ionized calcium binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba1), a marker of microglia. As expected, we observed no colocalization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry showing no colocalization with microglial markers

claim: There were no YFP+ cells in bone marrow isolated from Viaat-Cre;ROSA-YFP mice.
source: We also confirmed that there were no YFP+ cells in bone marrow isolated from Viaat-Cre;ROSA-YFP mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by FACS analysis of bone marrow

claim: MeCP2 expression in Viaat-Cre;Mecp2lox-Stop/Y mice colocalizes with GAD67-positive GABAergic neurons.
source: In the presence of the Viaat-Cre allele, however, the STOP cassette is excised and Mecp2 is transcribed normally in GABAergic neurons, as indicated by colocalization with the GABAergic neuron marker glutamic acid decarboxylase 67 (GAD67, Figure 1A left panel)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry showing colocalization

claim: CamKII-positive excitatory neurons in Viaat-Cre;Mecp2lox-Stop/Y mice remain null for MeCP2.
source: CamKII-positive excitatory neurons (Figure 1A right panel) remain null for MeCP2.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry showing no MeCP2 in CamKII+ neurons

claim: Male Viaat-Cre;Mecp2lox-Stop/Y rescue mice were indistinguishable from wildtype and Viaat-Cre littermates in appearance.
source: The Viaat-Cre;Mecp2lox-Stop/Y male mice (referred to hereafter as the 'rescue mice') appeared grossly indistinguishable from their wildtype and Viaat-Cre littermates (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated observation with supporting image

claim: Mecp2lox-Stop/Y mice became obese by seven weeks of life.
source: While Mecp2lox-Stop/Y mice became obese by seven weeks of life, the body weight of the rescue mice paralleled that of their wildtype and Viaat-Cre littermates (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by body weight measurements over time

claim: The body weight of male rescue mice paralleled that of their wildtype and Viaat-Cre littermates.
source: While Mecp2lox-Stop/Y mice became obese by seven weeks of life, the body weight of the rescue mice paralleled that of their wildtype and Viaat-Cre littermates (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by body weight measurements over time

claim: Male rescue mice lived significantly longer than their Mecp2lox-Stop/Y counterparts.
source: Male rescue mice lived significantly longer than their Mecp2lox-Stop/Y counterparts: no Mecp2lox-Stop/Y male mouse survived past 30 weeks of life, but 47% of the rescue mice survived past one year (22 out of 47 total rescue mice recorded) (Figure 1C).

claim: No Mecp2lox-Stop/Y male mouse survived past 30 weeks of life.
source: Male rescue mice lived significantly longer than their Mecp2lox-Stop/Y counterparts: no Mecp2lox-Stop/Y male mouse survived past 30 weeks of life, but 47% of the rescue mice survived past one year (22 out of 47 total rescue mice recorded) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by survival curve data

claim: 47% of the male rescue mice survived past one year.
source: Male rescue mice lived significantly longer than their Mecp2lox-Stop/Y counterparts: no Mecp2lox-Stop/Y male mouse survived past 30 weeks of life, but 47% of the rescue mice survived past one year (22 out of 47 total rescue mice recorded) (Figure 1C).

claim: Two male rescue mice reached two years of age.
source: Two rescue mice reached two years of age, which to our knowledge have never been reported with any manipulation of this model.
evidence: Stated observation from the study

claim: Rescue mice maintained their body weight throughout life, unlike Mecp2lox-Stop/Y males.
source: Rescue mice also maintained their body weight throughout life, unlike Mecp2lox-Stop/Y males, which tended to lose a significant percentage of their body weight in the weeks preceding death (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).

claim: No behavioral seizures were observed in any rescue mouse at any age.
source: We did not observe behavioral seizures in any rescue mouse at any age

claim: GABAergic-specific Mecp2 knockout mice develop pronounced ataxia early in life.

claim: Male rescue mice performed nearly as well as wildtype and Viaat-Cre littermates on the accelerating rotarod at six weeks of age.

claim: Male rescue mice performed nearly as well as wildtype and Viaat-Cre littermates on the grip strength assay at six weeks of age.

claim: Male rescue mice were not more active than the nulls in the open field assay at nine weeks of age.

claim: Mecp2lox-Stop/Y mice were unable to bury marbles at 9 weeks of age.
